# Code scout

Answers one question about one repository's code. You edit nothing and you search nowhere else.

You are given the repository's absolute path, the question, and optionally context on why it is being asked and whether test files are in scope (they are not by default).

## Read the layout first

Read the repository's `CLAUDE.md` or `README.md` when one exists, for how the code is laid out and what the parts are called. Use those names in your search patterns and target the directories they point at.

## Depth

The wording of the question tells you how deep to go.

- "Where", "find", "locate", "definition": find the thing, return it.
- "How", "flow", "calls", "uses": find it and trace what calls it and what it calls, far enough to answer.
- "End to end", "complete", "trace", "understand": follow the whole path and report each step.

When in doubt, go deeper. Missing a connection costs the caller a second dispatch.

## Scope

Only the repository you were given. Use `git -C <repo-path>` and absolute paths for everything; never `cd`. When the answer points outside the repository (an import from another package, a call to another service, a table another codebase owns), report the reference and where it points, and search nothing beyond the boundary.

## Output

Lead with the answer to the question in one to three sentences. Then the findings that support it, each with `path:line` (or `path:start-end`), one line on why it matters, and a snippet only when the code itself is the answer, trimmed to the lines that carry it. Verify every line number against the file before reporting it.

Then, only when they exist: references that leave the repository, and what you searched for and did not find.

Keep the whole report under forty lines. Long reports get cut in delivery. Report what is there; when nothing matches, say so and list the patterns you tried.

## Task

Repository: /home/agus/workspace/filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course (focus on app/). Question: where does this project keep (1) its code style / coding conventions for agents and humans, and (2) the routing of "when you change X, also update Y" (which doc, test or file to touch)? Check: app/AGENTS.md, any CLAUDE.md at any level, .claude/ (rules/, settings, commands, skills, agents), .mahou/ (basics.md, per-skill files, wiki/), .cursor/ or similar, lint configs (biome/eslint/oxlint/tsgo settings) that encode conventions, lefthook.yml, docs/README.md, CONTRIBUTING files. Quote the relevant rules briefly with paths. Report also what is NOT found. Under forty lines.
</supervisor-agent>

     5	This is the course material repository for "From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering", a 6-session extension course at FaMAF (Universidad Nacional de Cordoba). Target audience: ~30 CS students and junior programmers with some project experience but little professional training.
     6

    10	sessions/          — per-session materials (slides, exercises, instructor notes)
    11	  session-1/       — The Vibe Coding Experience        ┐

---
     1	---
     2	title: "kurasu: docs"
     3	summary: "The docs: what each folder holds, how files are named, and how to write a note."
     4	---
     5	
     6	# kurasu: docs
     7	
     8	## What each folder holds
     9	
    10	| Folder | Holds | Index |
    11	|---|---|---|
    12	| architecture/ | the shape of the system and how each part works | [Architecture](architecture/README.md) |
    13	| prototipos/ | no notes, only the HTML prototypes of the screens that the notes link to | [Prototipos](prototipos/README.md) |
    14	
    15	There is a single note folder, so every note goes in `architecture/`, whatever part of the system it explains.
    16	
    17	`_templates/` holds no notes. The underscore is a sorting convention and nothing more: it floats the folder to the top of the file explorer.
    18	
    19	`prototipos/` holds no notes either: it holds the HTML prototypes of the screens, and each one is linked from the note that describes its screen.
    20	
    21	## Naming
    22	
    23	A note is named after the aspect it explains, in kebab-case. Not after its folder, not numbered, not dated: a date is a frontmatter field, so an index can sort on it without every filename carrying one.
    24	
    25	File names are unique across the whole docs folder, so a link never has to be disambiguated. Before adding a note, check the name is not taken.
    26	
    27	Every folder's index is called `README.md`, so that name is the one deliberate collision here: the payoff is that each index renders as a folder front page when the repository is browsed on the web. A link to a folder's index names the folder: `[the technical design](technical-design/README.md)`.
    28	
    29	## Frontmatter
    30	
    31	Every note carries `title` and `summary`, plus `created`. The summary is what shows up in search, in hover previews and in the indexes, so write it as a sentence about the subject rather than about the note.
    32	
    33	## Invariants
    34	
    35	[`architecture/invariantes.md`](architecture/invariantes.md) lists the rules every change respects. The mahou skills read it before settling or proposing anything and check each decision against it. Add a rule when it holds beyond the change that surfaced it, and link the note that explains it when the reason needs more than a sentence.
    36	
    37	## How to write a note
    38	
    39	**A note explains how one part works.** It opens with an overview a reader can stop after, then the mechanism: the shape of the data, what calls what, in what order, with a diagram when the subject is a flow, a tree or a sequence. A reader should be able to hold that part of the system in their head without opening `src/` first.
    40	
    41	`_templates/note.md` offers the sections a note can use. They are a menu, not a required shape and not a closed list: keep the ones the subject needs, add one the menu lacks when the subject asks for it, and order them so the note is easiest to follow rather than in the order the template lists them. Edge cases and failure modes go in the prose or in a callout, never in a section of their own.
    42	
    43	**Reasoning goes in a callout, beside the thing it justifies**, not as the spine of the note:
    44	
    45	```markdown
    46	> [!NOTE] Why it is this way and not the obvious alternative
    47	> The reasoning, next to the mechanism it justifies.
    48	```
    49	
    50	A note that opens with the argument for a design makes the reader meet the case for the architecture before the architecture itself, and the argument is not what they came for. It is still worth keeping (it is what lets a decision be revisited rather than re-argued); it just is not the spine. Per-decision *why* is also the one thing the code already has, densely, at the point of each decision; what code cannot give anyone is the shape of the whole.
    51	
    52	Three callout kinds, and they mean different things:
    53	
    54	- `> [!NOTE]`: a real choice, and why it went that way.
    55	- `> [!WARNING]`: a failure mode: what breaks, how it presents, and whether anything catches it. Prefer failures that have actually happened.
    56	- `> [!TIP]`: an alternative considered and not taken, with the reason it was not.
    57	
    58	**A note is not a decision record.** There is no requirements table, no acceptance criteria, no user story, no status ladder. Those describe work being planned; a note describes something that exists.
    59	
    60	**A note describes the present.** No "used to", no "previously", no "no longer". An alternative that was rejected is *considered and not chosen, because…*, a standing reason, not a history of the argument. A note describes the system, not the state of its construction: no section on what is built, pending or planned.

     3	- [`architecture`](architecture.md): how kurasu's backend is split into core, adapters and apps, and the rules for errors, schemas, config, Alchemy and reads
     4	- [`api`](api.md): how kurasu's HTTP API is shaped: resources, student and admin routes, filters, embedded values, list and detail
     5	- [`web`](web.md): how kurasu's web is built: shared pieces with slots, API hooks with optimistic patches and error toasts, skeletons and the error screen, the shared button, confirmations and overlays, folders and styling
     6	- [`fence`](fence.md): the lint, type and commit checks that run on kurasu's code, and where its tests live
     7	- [`alchemy`](alchemy/INDEX.md): running an Alchemy 2 stack locally behind Vite and testing against it
     8	- [`browser`](browser/INDEX.md): what browser APIs expose to a page
# Test design in kurasu

- Automated tests are integration tests only, in the API and the web.
- A manual check is a web test row marked `test + manual`. Claude runs each one with agent-browser against the local stack. Every web branch has at least one. Pick the common cases, common errors included, such as a login with a user who has access and one who does not. Leave rare cases as tests only.
- API branches carry manual checks too: their most common rows, common errors included, marked `test + manual`. Claude runs each one against the local stack with HTTP requests, and checks the response and the state it leaves (the lists it changes, the mails the local binding writes). Leave rare cases as tests only.
- Checks that need production, such as the domain, real mail or hibernation, go in their own tree. Claude and the user run them by hand after the site launches on Cloudflare. They are not part of the design for the first implementation.

# Architecture

This folder holds the shape of the system and how each part works. Each note explains one part of it; the reasoning behind a choice sits in a callout next to the mechanism it justifies. See [the docs charter](../README.md) for how a note is written.

## What notes exist

One row per note, kept by hand: adding a note here is part of writing it.

| Note | Explains |
|---|---|
| [Modelo de datos](modelo-de-datos.md) | Las entidades que kurasu guarda en D1: usuarios, sesiones con su material, encuestas, preguntas, manos levantadas y novedades pendientes, y los códigos de registro y de los links del mail. |
| [Acceso a datos](acceso-a-datos.md) | Cómo la API lee y escribe en D1: el repositorio común sobre cada tabla, los puertos que el core declara con sus operaciones, las queries propias de cada store, y los límites de filas y de parámetros. |
| [Componentes](componentes.md) | Las piezas de kurasu y cómo se hablan: la web en el navegador, la API y el aula en Cloudflare, D1, R2, Email Sending y el estado que guarda el navegador. |
| [Login y acceso](login-y-acceso.md) | Cómo un usuario se registra y entra con un magic link, cómo la API revisa el acceso en cada pedido y cómo el profe administra los usuarios y el código de registro. |
| [Tiempo real del aula](tiempo-real-del-aula.md) | Cómo el aula de cada sesión avisa al instante sus cambios, quién cuenta como presente, qué pasa cuando se corta la conexión y cómo se comporta la pantalla del aula. |
| [API de las slides](api-de-las-slides.md) | Cómo la web le dice al HTML de las slides a qué slide y paso ir, cómo viaja la posición del profe hasta los estudiantes y cómo se revisa que un HTML respete la API al marcarlo como slides, desde el modal de subida o desde la lista del material. |
| [Estados de encuestas y sesiones, y sus pantallas](estados-de-encuestas-y-sesiones.md) | Los ciclos de vida de las encuestas, las sesiones y las preguntas, qué ve el estudiante en su inicio, cómo maneja el profe las sesiones desde el admin. |
| [Carga y acciones de la web](carga-y-acciones-de-la-web.md) | Cómo la web dibuja una pantalla mientras cargan sus datos, qué muestra cuando la carga falla y cómo responde a cada acción del usuario, al instante o en espera. |
| [Novedades por mail](novedades-por-mail.md) | Cómo kurasu registra lo nuevo de cada sesión como novedades pendientes, cómo el profe elige cuáles anunciar desde el admin de la sesión y cómo la API manda el anuncio por mail a los usuarios con acceso. |
| [Invariantes](invariantes.md) | Las reglas que respeta todo cambio en kurasu, sobre cómo se comporta el producto y cómo está armado el sistema. |

# kurasu: checks and tests

verified: 2026-10-22

Answers which checks reject code in kurasu and where its tests live.

## Knowledge

- oxlint runs type-aware with every rule as an error; oxfmt formats the code.
- A local plugin enforces boundaries: `apps/web` imports only `@kurasu/contract` and `@kurasu/slides` among the project's packages; `packages/core` imports no Cloudflare, Alchemy, Drizzle or jose; `packages/*` never import `apps/*`.
- TypeScript rules: `== null` instead of `=== null` or `=== undefined`; no enums (a const map and a derived type); named exports only.
- React rules: arrow-function components with a `Props` interface; React imported by name; conditional rendering with a ternary, never `&&`; no nested ternaries; one component per file; no destructured `useQuery` or `useMutation`.
- The project copies anti-slop into `tools/oxlint/anti-slop/` and adapts it as its own, with its generic and Effect rules.
- `@effect/tsgo` makes `tsc` fail on Effect diagnostics: missing services, `any` in error channels, global `Date`, `fetch` or `console` inside Effect.
- lefthook runs check on every commit; nobody commits with `--no-verify`. The tests run by hand with `pnpm test` before handing work over, because the API suite takes about a minute. turbo caches each package's tests until the package or one of its workspace dependencies changes.
- Tests are integration tests only, in `apps/api/test` (Alchemy's `alchemy/Test/Vitest` in dev mode, HTTP and WebSocket against the local stack) and `apps/web/test` (screens with the real router, the API answered by MSW, Testing Library on happy-dom). Tests live only there: the `test-location` lint rule rejects a test file anywhere else, and the root `projects` list names only the two apps. Before a package whose logic is too complex to cover through the API or the web gets its own tests, extend both the `test-location` rule and the root `projects` list to include it. Tests do not mock modules.
- Two web test helpers control when the mock server answers a request and what it answers. `heldResponse(method, path)` (`test/helpers/held-response.ts`) holds every request to the path until the test calls `release`, so the test can check the screen while the request is still waiting: a skeleton, a pending button. Released without a response, the requests fall through to the handlers already in place. `failingRoute(method, path, status = 500)` (`test/helpers/failing-route.ts`) answers the path with that status and a body no endpoint declares, as a failing server does.
- Pass the handlers that replace the page's own as the `overrides` argument of the test file's `openPage`, which calls `server.use` with them after the page's handlers and before the page renders. If the test calls `server.use` after the page opens, the requests that the page sends while it loads have already reached the page's handlers.
- On a machine under heavy load, some `/aula` tests can run past the 1 s that Testing Library's `findBy*` and `waitFor` wait by default. Run them again before changing them.
- Each API test file deploys its own stage: an empty D1 and R2, the migrations, and its fixtures loaded with `importFiles`. The tests in a file share that database, so each test uses its own records. The test stage sets `allowedDestinationAddresses` to the fixtures' emails; a link requested for an email outside the list makes the mail fail. A test reads the mail bodies from the files the local binding writes under `.alchemy/local/email`, and the sender, recipients and subject from the line the binding logs to the stage's Worker log under `.alchemy/log/<stage>/Api` (`test/helpers/sent-mail.ts`); see `alchemy/local-tests`.
- `app/vitest.config.ts` lists the two projects under Vitest 5's `projects` option; there is no `vitest.workspace.ts`. `happy-dom` and `msw` are also installed at the root, so the whole workspace resolves a single copy of vitest.
- The API project runs at most 4 test files at once (`maxWorkers: 4`): more stages starting together overload the local runtime and every file times out. Each run adds about 130 MB to `apps/api/.alchemy` (see `alchemy/local-tests`).
- The 101 MB upload test (A89) is skipped: under a full run the local runtime sometimes drops the connection mid-upload (EPIPE), and in production Cloudflare cuts a body past 100 MB before it reaches the Worker.
- There are no end-to-end tests. Rows marked `test + manual` in the test design are also run by hand with agent-browser against the local stack (`alchemy dev` and Vite).

## Sources

- `.scratch/aula-virtual/program-design/kurasu.md`, branch 9 and Standards.
- `.scratch/aula-virtual/research-tests-alchemy.md`.
- `.scratch/aula-virtual/research-stack-local.md` and `.scratch/aula-virtual/test-design/kurasu.md`.

**Answer:** Style lives mostly in the lint config (`app/.oxlintrc.json` plus custom rules under `app/tools/oxlint/`) and in the mahou wiki (`.mahou/wiki/`). There is no prose style guide. "When you change X, update Y" routing is a stub in `app/AGENTS.md` plus the docs charter. Paths below are relative to `/home/agus/workspace/filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course`.

**Conventions for agents and humans**
- `app/.oxlintrc.json:27-56` is the main encoding. `typeAware: true`, `denyWarnings: true`, and correctness and suspicious categories are errors.
  - `kurasu/null-check` and `kurasu/no-enum` are on, `eqeqeq` ignores null, and `import/no-default-export` is on.
  - Anti-slop rules include `no-object-parameters`, `no-unknown-returns`, `require-readable-spacing` and `require-safety-comment-for-type-assertion`.
  - Effect rules include `prefer-effect-match` and `no-manual-tag-comparison`.
- `app/.oxlintrc.json:58-75` has web-only overrides for `apps/web/**`: `kurasu/arrow-components`, `props-name`, `react-named-imports`, `ternary-render`, `no-destructured-query`, `no-nested-ternary`, `react/no-multi-comp`, `kurasu-boundaries/web-imports`.
- `app/.oxlintrc.json:76-91` has path overrides: `packages/core/**` gets `core-no-adapters` and `packages/**` gets `packages-no-apps`.
- `app/tools/oxlint/{kurasu,kurasu-boundaries,anti-slop}/` implement those rules. `tools/oxlint/anti-slop/UPSTREAM.md` marks anti-slop as copied and adapted.
- `.mahou/wiki/fence.md` is the prose summary of the checks.
  - Rules it lists: `== null`, no enums, named exports only, arrow components with `Props`, React named imports, ternaries and not `&&`, one component per file.
  - It also covers the layer boundaries and `@effect/tsgo`.
  - It says lefthook runs on every commit with no `--no-verify`, and that tests run by hand with `pnpm test`.
  - It says tests live only in `apps/api/test` and `apps/web/test`, enforced by the `kurasu/test-location` lint rule.
- `.mahou/wiki/{architecture,api,web}.md`, indexed by `.mahou/wiki/INDEX.md`, hold backend, HTTP and web conventions. I did not read their bodies.
- `.mahou/test-design.md` holds the test conventions: integration tests only, and `test + manual` rows run by hand with agent-browser.
- `app/.oxfmtrc.json` configures the formatter (oxfmt). It ignores `docs/**`, `**/migrations/**`, `routeTree.gen.ts` and anti-slop.
- `app/lefthook.yml:8-13` runs `pnpm check` on commits touching `app/**`. `app/package.json:7-8` defines check as lockfile check + varlock + typecheck + tools typecheck + `oxlint && oxfmt --check .`. `app/tools/hooks/install.sh` installs the hook.
- `CLAUDE.md` (root, 26 lines) covers the course content only: Spanish for student-facing material, Markdown, a README per exercise, and the session arc rules (don't move session 4's closing material into session 6). It has nothing about app code style.

**"When you change X, also update Y" routing**
- `app/AGENTS.md:12-14` has one entry under "When adding something": "A change to how a part of the app works → a note in `docs/architecture/`". It also says to read `docs/README.md` before adding, editing, renaming or moving anything under `docs/`.
- `app/docs/README.md` is the docs charter.
  - Naming: kebab-case, unique names, `created` and `title` frontmatter, and a note describes the present, not history.
  - Callouts: `[!NOTE]`, `[!WARNING]` and `[!TIP]`.
  - Line 35: `architecture/invariantes.md` lists rules every change respects, and a rule is added there when it holds beyond one change.
- `app/docs/architecture/README.md` keeps a hand-maintained note index ("adding a note here is part of writing it"). `app/docs/prototipos/README.md` is the same for prototypes, each linked from its note.
- `app/docs/_templates/note.md` is the note template.

**Not found**
- No `app/CLAUDE.md` and no nested `CLAUDE.md`.
- No `.claude/rules/`, `.claude/commands/` or `.claude/agents/`. `.claude/` holds only `settings.local.json` and `skills/session-replay`, which is unrelated to code style.
- No `.mahou/basics.md` and no per-skill files. `.mahou/` has only `test-design.md` and `wiki/`.
- No `.cursor/`, `CONTRIBUTING*` or `.github/`.
- No biome or eslint configs, and no tsgo settings in the root (tsconfigs only: `app/tsconfig.base.json` and per-package ones).
- No routing for changes to the API (`.mahou/wiki/api.md`), schema or migrations, tests, or slides API to docs. `AGENTS.md` has no code-style section, so conventions reach an agent only through lint failures or by reading the wiki.
- `.pi/` has `settings.json` and `agents/cc-plugins`. I did not open them.
- Not checked: the bodies of `invariantes.md` (only its first 15 lines) and of `.mahou/wiki/{architecture,api,web}.md`.
